title: AppLovin (APP) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript
transcript:
Record Q3 cash flow funded a larger buyback as gaming re-accelerated.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

DATE

Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026

CALL PARTICIPANTS

TAKEAWAYS

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email[email protected]

RISKS

SUMMARY

AppLovin Corporation(APP+29.83%)delivered record third-quarter results, reporting significant revenue growth and margin expansion driven by the deployment of next-generation advertising models. Management reported that a partial rollout of new model architecture has re-accelerated the core gaming business and continues to scale the consumer vertical, which is growing at triple-digit rates year over year. The company remains focused on utilizing its asset-light model to generate high cash flow conversion, supporting an aggressive shareholder return strategy that includes an expanded share repurchase authorization. Management indicated that even as investment in training compute increases, infrastructure optimizations are maintaining operational leverage and leading margins across the advertising sector.

INDUSTRY GLOSSARY

Full Conference Call Transcript

David Hsiao:Welcome to AppLovin's Earnings Call for the Third Quarter ended September 30, 2026. I'm David Hsiao, Head of Investor Relations. Joining me today to discuss our results are Adam Foroughi, our Co-Founder and CEO; and Matt Stumpf, our CFO. Please note our SEC filings to date, as well as our financial data and press release discussing our third quarter performance, are available at investors.applovin.com. During today's call, we will be making forward-looking statements, including but not limited to the future development and reach of our platform, our expected growth opportunities, the expected future financial performance of the company, and other future events.

These statements are based on our current assumptions and beliefs, and we assume no obligation to update them except as required by law. Our actual results may differ materially from the results predicted. We encourage you to review the risk factors in our most recently filed Form 10-Q for the fiscal quarter ended June 30th, 2026. Additional information may also be found in our quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the fiscal quarter ended September 30th, 2026, which will be filed today. We will also be discussing non-GAAP financial measures. These non-GAAP measures are not intended to be superior to or a substitute for our GAAP results.

Please be sure to review the GAAP results and the reconciliations of our GAAP and non-GAAP financial measures in our earnings release and financial update, available on our investor relations site. This conference call is being recorded, and a replay and transcript will be available for a period of time on our IR website. Now I'll turn it over to Adam and Matt for some opening remarks, then we'll have the moderator take us through Q&A.

Adam Foroughi:Thanks, everyone, for joining us today. We delivered a record quarter, revenue of $2.18 billion, up 55% year-over-year, the largest sequential dollar step-up in revenue, with well over $200 million more than last quarter. Both revenue and EBITDA came in well above the high end of our guidance. That's the standard we've always run this business by, outperforming our expectations. That result belongs to our team. They're carrying out a model transition as significant as Axon 2.0 while running the business at full speed, and they delivered both in the same quarter. I want to thank them. Here's what drove it.

During the quarter, we partially rolled out the next generation of our models, built on the architectural changes I described last quarter. Performance was strong. Advertisers saw more spend deploying profitably at their target return on ad spend goals, and budgets stepped up. Our gaming business grew nearly 50% year-over-year, re-accelerating right alongside the rollout. Here's the part I want you to sit with. This was a partial rollout. The transition is still in front of us, and the new generation gives us meaningfully more room to optimize than the architecture it replaces. It also improves performance most where data is sparser, newer advertisers, smaller advertisers, newer categories, exactly where our consumer vertical lives.

As always, model gains won't land on a perfect quarterly schedule, and we won't promise a cadence, but the headroom is real, and we're still very early. Just as important, we did it with discipline. While part of the team trained the new models, our engineers optimized how we serve them. So even as training investment increased, data center costs declined as a percentage of revenue. Every dollar of this investment is gated on return. In this quarter, you saw both halves of that, the return in revenue and the discipline in margin.

Consumer had another strong quarter, and with Q4 now underway, the seasonal peak for these advertisers, consumer is set up very well heading into the biggest spending season of the year. On the long term, nothing has changed. We run one auction across multiple advertiser categories. Gaming keeps improving, consumer keeps adding runway, and we believe this business can compound at roughly 30% annually over the long term. As this year shows, we intend to run well ahead of that whenever we can. Our focus heading into next year is consistent.

Complete the model transition and optimize on top of it, expand spend from our current customers while really ramping up the rate of acquiring new customers, keep improving our creative tools and ad formats, and start expanding our efforts on CTV. Let me close with this. A quarter ago, we stood here answering questions about a miss. We told you what had happened, that it was fixed, and that the business was re-accelerating, and everything we told you showed up in this quarter's numbers. That's how we'll keep operating, build for the long term, be transparent about challenges and opportunities, and compound through the noise. With that, I'll turn it over to Matt to walk through the financials.

Matt Stumpf:Thanks, Adam, and thanks to everyone for joining us today. AppLovin posted record third quarter earnings. Net income grew 72% year-over-year to $1.44 billion on record revenue of $2.18 billion, up 55% year-over-year, with an industry-leading 66% net income margin and 84% adjusted EBITDA margin. Revenue grew 14% sequentially and exceeded the high end of our guidance by approximately $100 million, primarily driven by the core mobile gaming business due to model improvements during the quarter, with continued scaling in the consumer vertical. Consumer advertisers' spend continues to have healthy growth, with spend up double digits quarter-over-quarter and growing triple digits from the same quarter last year.

Adjusted EBITDA was $1.84 billion, up 59% year-over-year, and also above the high end of our guidance range at an 84% margin, up approximately 190 basis points from the same period last year. Quarter-over-quarter flow through to adjusted EBITDA was 87%. Operating leverage remains strong. Our data center cost declined as a percentage of revenue due to optimizations rolled out by our infrastructure team, even as we invested in additional compute for training our existing models and for new model development. We manage this business to EBITDA dollars and free cash flow rather than to a margin percentage, and we'll continue to deploy dollars when we see an opportunity to produce more revenue.

Free cash flow for the quarter was $1.4 billion, or 77% of adjusted EBITDA, up from 53% in the second quarter. As I mentioned on last quarter's call, second quarter conversion was depressed by the timing of cash tax payments. We still expect full-year free cash flow conversion of roughly 70%-75% of adjusted EBITDA. To put our results in context, this earnings season, the largest platforms in digital advertising reported third quarter revenue growth between roughly 10% and the mid-20%s year-over-year. We grew 55%, several times faster than the market, and we did it at margins well above all of our peers across the advertising space. The contrast is even sharper on cash.

This quarter, our asset-light model converted roughly 65% of revenue into free cash flow. We ended the quarter with $3.17 billion of cash against $3.5 billion of long-term debt, which puts net leverage below 0.1 times adjusted EBITDA, comfortably below the roughly one times net leverage where we expect to operate over the long term. During the third quarter, we repurchased and withheld a total of 4.1 million shares for $1.4 billion, a meaningful step up from the second quarter, and ended the quarter with 331 million shares outstanding.

Given our continued confidence in the company's future, our board of directors increased our share repurchase authorization by an incremental $3.2 billion, bringing our total current authorization to $3.6 billion as of the end of October. Since we began the program, we have repurchased and withheld a total of 104 million shares for $9.4 billion at an average price of $90 per share, returning 85% of our free cash flow over that period and reducing our share count materially. Our weighted average diluted share count has now declined for eight consecutive quarters and is down approximately 2% from a year ago, even as we invest in the business.

That combination, 55% growth with a shrinking share count, is one very few companies can match. Turning to our outlook for the fourth quarter of 2026, we expect revenue between $2.365 billion and $2.395 billion, representing approximately 43%-44% year-over-year growth, or 8%-10% sequentially. We expect adjusted EBITDA between $1.995 billion and $2.025 billion, representing approximately 43%-45% year-over-year growth. At the midpoint, this guidance implies full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA growth of more than 50%. That outlook reflects normal seasonality, further scaling in our consumer vertical, significant model improvements that are already live and performing, and continued investment in training compute for new model development.

To close, we exceeded the high end of our guidance on both revenue and adjusted EBITDA, grew revenue 55% year-over-year, expanded margins, generated $1.4 billion of free cash flow, and returned $1.4 billion to shareholders. Our fourth quarter outlook reflects that same trajectory. With that, let's move to Q&A.

Operator:We will now begin the question and answer session. Please be sure to unmute and turn on your video before asking your question. We will take as many questions as time permits. Since we have many questions today, please be patient as we move through the list. Our first question will come from James Heaney. Please unmute and ask your question.

James Heaney:Yeah, great. Just a couple from me. I will start with Adam. Could you just talk about these new generations of models that you are rolling out? Just curious what the biggest improvement that you see is compared to Axon 2, and then anything around just timing of the full rollout, and then I will ask one to Matt.

Adam Foroughi:Yeah. Hey, James. We talked about it last quarter, but one of our objectives was try to get to a place where we could build bigger models, use more compute, and try to train a model that has better output. So, I foreshadowed it for you last quarter. We are now starting to roll those out. We have seen good results. We cannot tell you or commit to when we can actually see a full rollout or how the progression of these models will go, but what I said in the talk track is, these models have a lot more room to optimize them than the old generation that we were on. So, we are really excited about the future.

James Heaney:Great. Then one for Matt. Just on the surface, it feels like the Q4 revenue guide of the 8%-10% sequential growth seems a bit more conservative versus the 14% in Q3 when you layer in the strength of e-commerce in the quarter for Q4. Just how would you frame up that sequential deceleration?

Matt Stumpf:Yeah, I mean, our guidance philosophy remains the same from what we've done over the past few quarters. We're guiding to what we know at that point in time. So, we're guiding to include the points that I said in my script, which are normal seasonality within the quarter, the model updates that we've already launched and are live and performing, and then obviously the increase in the data center cost. So, nothing there has really changed from previous quarters.

James Heaney:Thank you.

Operator:Your next question comes from Jason Bazinet with Citi. Please go ahead.

Jason Bazinet:One question. Last quarter you guys talked about leaning into the referral program a bit more. I was just wondering if you could give us an update on whether you're pleased or not with the progress you're making with those partners. Thanks.

Adam Foroughi:Yeah. Hey, Jason. Still a work in progress. Obviously, this is going to be multi-quarter, multi-year trajectory on this business. We're early in doing partnerships, but as you've seen, even in the rate of pixel counts that I think you're publishing, is that we've been getting more and more customers coming on, and the rate is accelerating. That's only going to compound over time, because not only are you going to have more partnership deals, we'll start running more ad campaigns, but you're just going to have more positive sentiment on the product in the market as more customers start getting a good experience and doing it over time.

Because the other thing you got to realize is, we got customers that come on, they have to get campaigns that are scaled and optimized on our platform, they have to run an incrementality study, they have to prove that it works, and then they really scale for the long term. So, we expect this stuff will just keep compounding over time.

Jason Bazinet:Thanks.

Operator:Our next question will come from Matthew Cost with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Matthew Cost:Great. Thanks for taking the question. I guess, does the experience that you've had with this new model that just rolled out, does that change your expectations for how much runway there still is ahead to improve gaming ad revenue? Because you've been relatively specific over the course of this year about a 20%-30% growth expectation and sort of law of large numbers weighing on gaming. Would you reiterate all of that at this point, or is there potentially more headroom than you would have otherwise expected based on how it's gone so far?

Adam Foroughi:I mean, what we've been specific on the last two quarters that we're committed to is an expectation that we can grow this business 30% year-over-year for the long term. We are a platform that's a unified auction. Let's say in some world, we grew consumer 1,000% in the next quarter. That's going to create more competition, right? You can't look at it verticalized as this consumer business is now growing more and more. It's very hard to judge a vertical by itself in a silo. That said, this model is for sure more accurate than the old model, and it has a lot more room to optimize going forward.

If we're able to do that, of course, we would expect that gaming could continue to grow at higher rates for the long term. It's just not something that we need, though, in order to hit that 30% if we have both parts of the business growing pretty quickly. As we touched on in the talk track, the other side of the business, the consumer side, is growing triple digits. When you have a business like that now isn't immaterial in our business, growing at that rate with a lot of opportunity to grow in the future as we go get more customer penetration, it gives us a lot of headroom on future growth opportunity.

Matthew Cost:Got it. Thank you. I noticed you mentioned CTV in the prepared remarks. I think it's been a little while since that's something you chose to highlight. I guess, how prominently does that feature into your product roadmap right now relative to six months ago?

Adam Foroughi:Yeah, we're making more progress there. I mean, if people watch anything on connected television, you'll start seeing some of our ads. We've got pilot campaigns going now. The product is actually looking very promising. It's early. It's a whole new market, so I wouldn't bank on it at all for being accretive to numbers anytime soon. It's something that the team is actually gaining a lot of confidence in with where they're at in the product roadmap. If we get to the point where it actually starts showing really good results for customers, we'll talk about it more. Internally, we're now very excited about it.

Matthew Cost:Great. Thank you.

Operator:Next, we'll go to Benjamin Black with Deutsche Bank.

Benjamin Black:Great. Thank you for taking my question. Adam, you've spoken in the past the need to collect more data on the consumer side to refine the model and to improve performance, and then the flywheel around that. With the new architecture, do you have sort of line of sight to potentially getting the flywheel to reach a sort of a tipping point to where you were with gaming a few years back? If not, which incremental investments do you think are required?

Adam Foroughi:Look, these two things go hand in hand, right? Every day that we stay in business, we get customers that come into the platform, they share data with us, so we get more data density. As you fast-forward that quarters, years, you then need to pair it with model architecture that can actually process more data and generate better output. You write a bigger model, more complex model, you train it on a larger compute cluster, and you end up with better output. What this new architecture allows us to do on the gaming side and on the consumer side is just train bigger models. We're going to be starved for data.

The more data we get into the system quicker, the better the output of our predictions model is going to become. We're never going to stop looking to go get data, whether it's promoting ourselves through referrals and advertising, as we just touched on, for new customers, or potentially some sort of data acquisition. We're going to be looking for ways to get data into this model because we've seen every single time we add more data, we're able to write a more complex model, we're able to train a bigger model, and just get a better output on the other side.

Benjamin Black:Great. I guess, are consumer advertiser budgets shaping up for the holiday shopping season relative to last year? If you think advertisers see strong returns this quarter, how much of that spend could ultimately prove sticky into 2027, or should we expect a seasonal reset as usual in Q1?

Adam Foroughi:I think it just follows the normal patterns. I mean, look, we're still early in the curve. It's not even into the holiday season, so that stuff takes form really over the next couple of weeks. But that seasonal reset, I mean, that's consistent in e-comm. Now, we do have the benefit that so long as we're growing this business at this rate and we're pretty early in its evolution, we still have rate of customer acquisition allowing us to grow the business, even in more traditionally seasonally difficult quarters like the Q1 versus Q4 comp. But that said, the same advertiser, like for like, will have a huge Q4 and follow it up with a weak Q1.

That's just the reality of the e-commerce business. Traditionally, if you looked at the business growth sequentially in our business, our Q1s have been pretty strong because gaming has a phenomenon called Q5, where going into Q1, they know that there's not as much competition. So the models, whether just selecting gaming more often because return on ad spend is compelling, or the customers being willing to take bigger risks because they're coming off of a very high-priced Q4 into this post-Q4 season, they end up spending very competitively. So, we've been more insulated than other advertising companies, but as we get more deep into e-commerce, we should see bigger Q4s followed by tougher Q1s.

Benjamin Black:Great. Thank you very much.

Operator:For our next question, we will go to Stephen Ju with UBS.

Stephen Ju:Hey, thanks. Hi, Adam. Hi, Matt. Thanks for taking the time. I think I was talking to some of the advertisers on your platform, and they said something curious. They were anticipating that the pricing on the auction is going to start getting inflated because you are going to have incremental bidders from e-commerce coming in and taking up the prices. They were preemptively taking some of the budgets to some of your competitors in anticipation of what might be compression of ROI.

Which kind of seemed like a strange thing to do, but it did make me worry about, I guess, the amount of inventory, which I think you have addressed in prior periods of this being, I guess, a demand-constrained industry as opposed to a supply-constrained industry. Can you talk about how your thinking might have evolved or things have changed at all in terms of AppLovin's ability to absorb all this incremental ad spend without having some of the ROI get compressed for some of your incumbent customers? Thanks.

Adam Foroughi:Yeah, I mean, if you look at our business over the last three years, we've gotten a lot more competitive. The business is much, much bigger. The ROI or return on ad spend for customers is stronger than it was three years ago because the spend is materially larger, right? The better these models get at taking an impression and predicting an outcome, the more accurate they can price.

Our step up this quarter in net revenue dollars against the last quarter, I don't know how much of our competition that's publicly reporting has in terms of scale to directly compare to that, but I think it's a lot of their annual reported revenue that we just put up in one quarter of growth. I think these industry checks tend to end up being flawed because you're looking at a small sub-segment of the ecosystem, and the customers that are taking time talking to you all probably aren't working that hard. The ones that are working hard and succeeding probably aren't talking to you all.

I would say we're a pretty good indicator on the market, and our technology has proven to be great at getting better pricing for customers. That doesn't mean that just looking at a CPM, the price is not going up. In fact, if we get better targeted so that our conversion rate goes up, the CPM will go up. But the down funnel effect of a better prediction is that the return on ad spend is going up, and that's why we're able to grow so quickly.

Stephen Ju:Thank you.

Operator:Next question, we'll hear from Robert Coolbrith with Evercore.

Robert Coolbrith:Hey, thank you for the opportunity to ask a question. I just wanted to ask a little bit more about the architecture. Is that something, as it becomes larger or allows for more data and models get bigger, is that something that also becomes more generalizable? I know in the past you've talked about keeping the consumer and the gaming model separate, but is that something where the models become sort of more generalizable across media types, across client types over time?

Adam Foroughi:Yeah, it's possible. Oh, sorry to interrupt on the second question, but you're right. It is possible that we will eventually be able to take this architecture that direction.

Robert Coolbrith:Okay, got it. I just wanted to ask a little bit about maybe brand performance, if you will. We're hearing from more brands, maybe because of the issues in mobile web, both in terms of inventory supply, but also iOS 26, focus more on mobile app inventory. Do you see that as an opportunity that's potentially attractive or interesting for AppLovin going forward?

Adam Foroughi:I mean, certainly if it's a performance marketer. So, I would split up performance brand into true performance where they're optimizing the incremental ROAS or like a down funnel purchase transaction. Then you've got performance brand that still is looking for audience reach. A lot of the mobile web advertising and a lot of what's called, I guess, traditionally open web, is more of the latter. They're just trying to buy audience and trying to price effectively as cheap as possible to reach that audience. We try to price the discovery all the way to the point of transaction.

So, if that's what they care about and they're able to track it all on digital, then yes, we think a lot of those dollars will shift into the app space. It clearly performs really well. It's much, much bigger. I mean, I said this, I think, on the All-In pod at the All-In Summit, the scale of this space is getting very, very large. You can back into the gross spend numbers that we have, and they are pretty substantial. If you then gross that up for the whole space, this is one of the largest advertising opportunities that there are outside of social and search, maybe the largest outside of social and search.

We fully expect more dollars will follow given the performance is there.

Robert Coolbrith:Great. Thank you.

Operator:Our next question comes from Clark Lampen with BTIG.

Clark Lampen:Hey, guys. Good evening. I had two, if I may. I guess, Adam, I sort of wanted to pull at this model thread, and based on everything that I understand about where you guys are going right now, I think one of the bigger derivative benefits of success would be opening up a lot more inventory or available inventory, I guess, within the same sort of base of games and supply that you have right now, which probably should get filled because of auction dynamics by non-gaming advertisers. Is that right?

I guess just sort of number one, as we think about the second order benefits beyond just sort of more ads per 100 that you are buying right now translating to revenue generating customers for a commerce or gaming developer. If so, I guess, is there a way to frame for us just how significant, I guess, this sort of available or effective supply expansion could be?

Adam Foroughi:Yeah, I mean, look, I think the challenge with supply expansion is that the MAX market or the gaming advertising market is a lot bigger than people realize. When you've got this market that's in the tens of billions, we can go get new supply. In fact, this model that we're now on and that consumer vertical growing gives us a lot of opportunity to go get more supply. There aren't that many supply sources that are sort of open to third parties that could be a huge needle mover in one shot. Then you'd need to compound it over time.

The reason CTV is compelling to us is there's not a true top of funnel to bottom of funnel performance offering on connected TV. If we can figure that out and be the first to market with something that's scalable there's a lot of available inventory that's under monetized there. It's sort of what mobile looked like to us 10, 15 years ago when we started the business. Something like that could be impactful. Anything else, not so much. That's why we've always talked about this conversion rate. We're still very low on what we think is the possible conversion rate inside this gaming ecosystem. What consumer gives us is the chance to diversify the ads that someone's seeing.

Instead of showing the same user 20 gaming ads in a week, we might show them 15 product ads and five gaming ads. That doesn't mean that the gaming customers lost 75%. It just means that the model can get much more targeted, so those same five impressions that would have driven the conversion are still going to sit there, and now all of a sudden you have all these product ads. That's really the focus area. That's the largest needle mover in the short, medium term. Long term, for sure, supply expansion is something that we're going to be focused on.

Clark Lampen:Okay. That makes sense. For Matt, I guess just sort of net of what I think we were seeing just a moment ago in terms of after-hours share price reaction, your stock is still down ballpark 40% year-to-date, and it's only retraced most of the sort of post 2Q earnings step-down. Does the buyback give you flexibility, or the added authorization that you guys just layered on give you flexibility to be more aggressive, I guess, and opportunistic? If you think that the share price is meaningfully disconnected from intrinsic value, or is this mostly going to be programmatic going forward?

Matt Stumpf:No, I mean, you saw within the quarter as well, Clark, that we did a meaningful step-up, and so that was directly as a result of what you're referring to, right? That was us opportunistically ramping up the buyback because we saw this dislocation in the stock price versus the actual intrinsic value of the company. So, we have the ability to do that going forward as well.

Clark Lampen:Thank you, guys.

Matt Stumpf:Yeah.

Operator:Next, we'll go to Martin Yang with [Oppenheimer].

Martin Yang:Hi. Thank you for taking my question. A question for Adam. At an industry conference, you referenced that dynamic product ad for e-commerce sometimes can work better than video. I want to get your thoughts on the longer term. Do you think a more diversified ad format is the ultimate goal to make e-commerce more effective, or are you still just waiting on gen AI video creation to make volume and the quality of video ads higher, and this dynamic product ad is just an intermittent step for your advertisers to get volume in front of customers?

Adam Foroughi:Look, I'd say it's both. I mean, as the large language models that are applied to creative continuously improve, and there's a lot of companies in this ecosystem building ads now out of the box, you're going to see better advertiser performance. We're also going to create more ad formats that can service the advertisers in hopefully better ways. What we want is diversity of what the consumer sees. When you serve as many ads a day as we do, that diversity of content can create an uplift. That's why in my talk track, that was one of the bullets. It's an area of focus for us. This product is still really new.

I mean, I know we're a couple years in, but it's a really new product. The ad format hasn't evolved that much yet. I would fully expect it to evolve a lot more over the next couple of years.

Martin Yang:Got it. A follow-up on e-comm, if I may. When you compare this year going into the holiday season versus last year, how would you say the learning budget or learning time is for e-comm customers? How has that improved, if any?

Adam Foroughi:Yeah, I mean, look, learning is two-sided. So, our model has gotten better, and this new model architecture also, as I said in the talk track, is faster when there's less data. On the other hand, customers are risk-averse going into a new relationship. So, when they buy on us, even if the result looks better, they still need to validate it. So, in this category, if you talk to the customers, not only do they want to see spend and return on ad spend, they need to run incrementality studies too. So, there is a slow ramp-up. That's just a fact of the industry. But our product is getting better.

Every quarter that we go on and we have a new release, part of the space of getting it better is just improving it for current customers. The other space of getting it better is that, so a customer now clicks in, they don't have much data on our system, how quickly can you show them a good result? Because that's how you lower your churn rates.

Martin Yang:Thank you.

Operator:Next question will come from Rob Sanderson with Loop Capital.

Rob Sanderson:Yeah, thank you. Good afternoon, everybody. Couple questions on consumer as well. Growing triple digits, obviously, good trajectory here. Any commentary on conversion of new leads coming through self-service or through your referral partners, or any specifics on customer outcomes? I am just kind of wondering, there is still a bit of hit and miss, kind of depending on sophistication of the advertiser. Are we still seeing similar trends, or anything you can comment on how the go-to-market is progressing?

Adam Foroughi:Yeah, I mean, look, we are still early in the product. If a customer goes through our team, much higher likelihood to succeed than they just go through self-service channel and they are on their own. Now, if they go through self-service and they are on their own and they are sophisticated, they absolutely can have success. If they are a very small business, something that is just what you would classify as complete SMB, that is still further into the future for us. There is a roadmap on this thing where the more data you get into the system, the more predictive you can be in the absence of data.

And we are not at the point yet where somebody can just plug in tiny business selling jewelry, we have never seen them before, very little data, very little GMV, and it just plugs in and they go. But five years from now, if we have got a lot of scale of data and the model has time to get evolved to the point of five years from now, you are going to have much better outcomes across the board. This is a roadmap. I mean, we got to build this product out over time to tackle every single circumstance. It is working really well for the customers that we either handhold or they come in and are sophisticated.

Rob Sanderson:Is ad creative still a primary barrier? That was a lot of the points of failure, a lot of things that were not working, it is kind of stalled out at the ad creative. Is that still kind of the primary sticking point? And if we kind of asked this question a year ago, I mean, did you expect the industry to be a little further ahead on gen AI tools by this point, one year ago? It seems like, to me at least, maybe things are a little bit slower than we would have thought.

Adam Foroughi:Yeah, and look, on the latter, the large language model companies in the West are focused on something else, and so you have less R&D outside of us on this problem. On the former, I wouldn't call it a barrier, but it is an opportunity cost or opportunity lost for customers that don't invest in creative. If you talk to customers that buy on Meta, they buy on TikTok, they buy on us, there's a constant point that they make that you need to put more creatives into AppLovin to have success on our platform. The ones that know that have more success than the ones that don't know that. The ones that don't might be smaller.

It's probably not a barrier to working at all, but they're missing a point of scale. The challenge is that our ads are just much longer, and they are seen. When you go into another platform and you load 10 ads, they're not seen that long, and a lot of them aren't seen. You load 10 ads into our platform, on average, you're getting over 35 seconds of watch time. User can't do anything else on the screen. It's a full-screen ad. They are being seen with 100% certainty. Ad count and quality of ad combination is what creates scale on our platform. Some customers know it. They're able to become our large spenders. The others have to learn it.

Rob Sanderson:I'm going to try to sneak one more in. You're talking about significantly larger models, right? Step function in scale. Are you generating enough data organically to feed the models? That exact X is the ownership of the advertising company, the company that wrote a model that processed a ton of data, has a relationship with customers and consumers to show an advertisement. That is their data. It is an output of their models. That remains with them. There is nothing that gives us magical data access from the mediation. In fact, when we built MAX, what we did was we commoditized it all. We said everyone is going to have the same access to data as we will as a bidder into MAX, because what we wanted was a fair marketplace.

The reason MAX out-monetizes the rest of the world of mobile gaming is because we made it fair, and that fairness is what drove the price of every single impression to be the highest possible.

Tim Nollen:Okay. That answered it.

Adam Foroughi:Did I answer your question?

Tim Nollen:Thanks very much, Adam. Yes, I got it. Thank you.

Operator:Take our last question from Matthew Swanson with RBC.

Matthew Swanson:Oh, great. Thanks for squeezing me in. Congratulations on the quarter. I guess on the consumer side, Adam, you mentioned there is some handholding in terms of the initial on-ramp if you are not a more sophisticated customer. I guess a two-parter there. One, how much of it is on you versus them in terms of improving that initial performance? Is it still about the models, or is it about them learning how to better optimize their usage of the platform? Secondarily, when you are targeting customers, it seems like these real sophisticated users are the more likely to generate revenue immediately. Is that more the priority, or are you looking for the best long-term partners for AppLovin?

Adam Foroughi:Yeah. I think a lot of this is a learning curve. We are a new platform, so a lot of these customers have not bought in games. They are not used to an ad that actually gets watched, and certainly not used to an ad that is watched for that much time. If you have a shop, I mean, think about, sometimes I think about, we are asking the customer to create 60 seconds of content to showcase a shop. I mean, what are you even showing that ad? It is like shops aren't that exciting. On the gaming side, they are creating mini-games, so someone is playing a preview of their game. It is straightforward.

There is a learning process here that has to happen so that the media buyers really understand the framework. Then once they do, and more and more media buyers understand it, and more agencies are trained, then it will become standardized. There will be playbooks for our platform. It is not dissimilar to buying on social 10 years ago. It was brand new. The scale was way smaller. People didn't know what to do. Now everyone knows what to do, because if you don't, you are probably not scaling your business. On the priority of the type of customers we go for, we are looking for the more sophisticated ones.

That is why these partnership deals make a lot of sense. Rather than just run AppLovin Ads everywhere, through strategic partnership deals, we can get real customers coming on.

Operator:That concludes the question and answer session for this quarter. We thank you all for joining us today. Have a good afternoon.

Adam Foroughi:Thanks, everyone, for joining us today. We delivered a record quarter, revenue of $2.18 billion, up 55% year-over-year, the largest sequential dollar step-up in revenue, with well over $200 million more than last quarter. Both revenue and EBITDA came in well above the high end of our guidance. That's the standard we've always run this business by, outperforming our expectations. That result belongs to our team. They're carrying out a model transition as significant as Axon 2.0 while running the business at full speed, and they delivered both in the same quarter. I want to thank them. Here's what drove it.

During the quarter, we partially rolled out the next generation of our models, built on the architectural changes I described last quarter. Performance was strong. Advertisers saw more spend deploying profitably at their target return on ad spend goals, and budgets stepped up. Our gaming business grew nearly 50% year-over-year, re-accelerating right alongside the rollout. Here's the part I want you to sit with. This was a partial rollout. The transition is still in front of us, and the new generation gives us meaningfully more room to optimize than the architecture it replaces. It also improves performance most where data is sparser, newer advertisers, smaller advertisers, newer categories, exactly where our consumer vertical lives.

As always, model gains won't land on a perfect quarterly schedule, and we won't promise a cadence, but the headroom is real, and we're still very early. Just as important, we did it with discipline. While part of the team trained the new models, our engineers optimized how we serve them. So even as training investment increased, data center costs declined as a percentage of revenue. Every dollar of this investment is gated on return. In this quarter, you saw both halves of that, the return in revenue and the discipline in margin.

Consumer had another strong quarter, and with Q4 now underway, the seasonal peak for these advertisers, consumer is set up very well heading into the biggest spending season of the year. On the long term, nothing has changed. We run one auction across multiple advertiser categories. Gaming keeps improving, consumer keeps adding runway, and we believe this business can compound at roughly 30% annually over the long term. As this year shows, we intend to run well ahead of that whenever we can. Our focus heading into next year is consistent.

Complete the model transition and optimize on top of it, expand spend from our current customers while really ramping up the rate of acquiring new customers, keep improving our creative tools and ad formats, and start expanding our efforts on CTV. Let me close with this. A quarter ago, we stood here answering questions about a miss. We told you what had happened, that it was fixed, and that the business was re-accelerating, and everything we told you showed up in this quarter's numbers. That's how we'll keep operating, build for the long term, be transparent about challenges and opportunities, and compound through the noise. With that, I'll turn it over to Matt to walk through the financials.

Matt Stumpf:Thanks, Adam, and thanks to everyone for joining us today. AppLovin posted record third quarter earnings. Net income grew 72% year-over-year to $1.44 billion on record revenue of $2.18 billion, up 55% year-over-year, with an industry-leading 66% net income margin and 84% adjusted EBITDA margin. Revenue grew 14% sequentially and exceeded the high end of our guidance by approximately $100 million, primarily driven by the core mobile gaming business due to model improvements during the quarter, with continued scaling in the consumer vertical. Consumer advertisers' spend continues to have healthy growth, with spend up double digits quarter-over-quarter and growing triple digits from the same quarter last year.

Adjusted EBITDA was $1.84 billion, up 59% year-over-year, and also above the high end of our guidance range at an 84% margin, up approximately 190 basis points from the same period last year. Quarter-over-quarter flow through to adjusted EBITDA was 87%. Operating leverage remains strong. Our data center cost declined as a percentage of revenue due to optimizations rolled out by our infrastructure team, even as we invested in additional compute for training our existing models and for new model development. We manage this business to EBITDA dollars and free cash flow rather than to a margin percentage, and we'll continue to deploy dollars when we see an opportunity to produce more revenue.

Free cash flow for the quarter was $1.4 billion, or 77% of adjusted EBITDA, up from 53% in the second quarter. As I mentioned on last quarter's call, second quarter conversion was depressed by the timing of cash tax payments. We still expect full-year free cash flow conversion of roughly 70%-75% of adjusted EBITDA. To put our results in context, this earnings season, the largest platforms in digital advertising reported third quarter revenue growth between roughly 10% and the mid-20%s year-over-year. We grew 55%, several times faster than the market, and we did it at margins well above all of our peers across the advertising space. The contrast is even sharper on cash.

This quarter, our asset-light model converted roughly 65% of revenue into free cash flow. We ended the quarter with $3.17 billion of cash against $3.5 billion of long-term debt, which puts net leverage below 0.1 times adjusted EBITDA, comfortably below the roughly one times net leverage where we expect to operate over the long term. During the third quarter, we repurchased and withheld a total of 4.1 million shares for $1.4 billion, a meaningful step up from the second quarter, and ended the quarter with 331 million shares outstanding.

Given our continued confidence in the company's future, our board of directors increased our share repurchase authorization by an incremental $3.2 billion, bringing our total current authorization to $3.6 billion as of the end of October. Since we began the program, we have repurchased and withheld a total of 104 million shares for $9.4 billion at an average price of $90 per share, returning 85% of our free cash flow over that period and reducing our share count materially. Our weighted average diluted share count has now declined for eight consecutive quarters and is down approximately 2% from a year ago, even as we invest in the business.

That combination, 55% growth with a shrinking share count, is one very few companies can match. Turning to our outlook for the fourth quarter of 2026, we expect revenue between $2.365 billion and $2.395 billion, representing approximately 43%-44% year-over-year growth, or 8%-10% sequentially. We expect adjusted EBITDA between $1.995 billion and $2.025 billion, representing approximately 43%-45% year-over-year growth. At the midpoint, this guidance implies full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted EBITDA growth of more than 50%. That outlook reflects normal seasonality, further scaling in our consumer vertical, significant model improvements that are already live and performing, and continued investment in training compute for new model development.

To close, we exceeded the high end of our guidance on both revenue and adjusted EBITDA, grew revenue 55% year-over-year, expanded margins, generated $1.4 billion of free cash flow, and returned $1.4 billion to shareholders. Our fourth quarter outlook reflects that same trajectory. With that, let's move to Q&A.

James Heaney:Thank you.

Jason Bazinet:One question. Last quarter you guys talked about leaning into the referral program a bit more. I was just wondering if you could give us an update on whether you're pleased or not with the progress you're making with those partners. Thanks.

Jason Bazinet:Thanks.

You can't look at it verticalized as this consumer business is now growing more and more. It's very hard to judge a vertical by itself in a silo. That said, this model is for sure more accurate than the old model, and it has a lot more room to optimize going forward.

If we're able to do that, of course, we would expect that gaming could continue to grow at higher rates for the long term.
